The daemon is using about 2–2.6 cores right now. After the October 28 fixes it settled at 0.66–0.90 cores. The session history has grown from about 5,600 to 13,505 sessions since then (66 running). The biggest cost I found is work that grows with the size of that history.

## What I measured
Live daemon: PID 2087559, version 2.68.0, up 4 h 20 min.

| Measurement | Result |
|---|---|
| 30 s average | 265% CPU: 117% user, 147% system |
| Per thread (15 s) | 320 `tokio-rt-worker` threads together 151%; `sessionwiki-sync` 55%; database writer 6% |
| Profile (perf, 20 s, user code only) | `memcmp` 13%, `SnapshotMap::filtered` inside `for_subagent_parents` 6.4%, B-tree lookups and `retain` key lists about 7%, malloc/free about 12% |
| Debugger stack samples | 2 of 3 samples caught `handle_action → runtime_changes_for_subagent_parents → for_subagent_parents` |

## What could reduce CPU, in order of likely gain

**1. Dashboard runtime polls (confirmed as the main hot path).** Each poll from the dashboard calls `frame_for_subagent_parents` (`mj-controller/src/daemon/feed.rs:90`). That calls `for_subagent_parents` (`mj-client/src/runtime_feed.rs:68`) twice, once for the current snapshot and once for the client's previous one. Each call:
- filters all 13,505 records;
- clones the other maps and removes non-matching keys from them one at a time.

The dashboard's next poll rebuilds the same "before" snapshot it got last time. The two rebuilt maps also share no B-tree leaves, so `RuntimeDelta::between` cannot skip unchanged parts. It compares every key and value, which is likely where the `memcmp` time comes from. `RuntimeSessionView` and `SessionTail` derive only `PartialEq`, not `Eq`. So comparing them likely cannot use the shortcut of first checking whether both sides point to the same data.

Possible fixes:
- Keep the scoped snapshot for each sequence number and family set, so the "before" side is not rebuilt.
- Better: build the new scoped snapshot from the previous one plus the changes in the full snapshot. Then the maps share structure and the diff costs only what changed.

**2. SessionWiki indexing (confirmed, about 0.55 core all the time).** `sessionwiki::index::index_one` (sessionwiki 0.34.5) deletes every full-text row of a changed session and inserts them all again. With 66 running sessions, the indexer keeps rewriting long transcripts. Indexing only the new messages would fix this, but the change belongs in the sessionwiki crate. A simpler option is to sync running sessions less often.

**3. Thread count (likely to help; gain not measured).** See your second question below.

**4. Small extras (confirmed, low CPU).** Every ~5 seconds the daemon re-checks 11 old child questions whose parents are stopped, and logs a warning each time (28,000 lines so far). It has also logged "park finished outcome=Busy" 8,400 times, which looks like park attempts on busy sessions being retried.

## Your questions

**What does ≈50% system time imply?** About half the CPU is spent in the kernel on the daemon's behalf, not in mj's own code. I could not see kernel stacks, because this host only allows profiling user code. So the cause is unknown. Likely contributors:
- Threads going to sleep and waking up. I measured about 19,000 context switches per second.
- Memory allocation churn: 12% of user time is malloc/free, and the process holds 11.6 GB of memory.
- SQLite reads and fsyncs.
- This WSL VM tends to report extra system time (from earlier notes).

The user-code work in items 1 and 2 also causes much of the allocation and wake-up traffic. Fixing those should reduce both kinds of time.

**320 tokio threads?** Yes, that is a lot:
- 120 are async worker threads. The daemon's runtime (`mj-cli/src/main.rs:551`) does not set `worker_threads`, so tokio starts one worker per CPU, and this VM has 120 vCPUs.
- About 200 are blocking-pool threads, started on demand for things like transcript paging, checkpoint compression and project-memory encoding. Each one exits after about 10 seconds idle.

The daemon mostly waits on I/O, so it does not need 120 workers. Idle workers still wake up to look for tasks to take from busy workers, which adds context switches and system time. Setting `worker_threads` to something like 8–16 is a one-line change worth measuring.

My recommendation is to start with item 1, then try the thread limit and measure again. I have not changed any code. The evidence (`profile.data`, debugger samples, `diagnosis.txt`) is in `/mnt/optane/tmp/mj-cpu-20261106/`.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The runtime snapshots are stored in persistent B-trees (`imbl`). Comparing two of them is cheap only when they share tree nodes, because shared nodes can be skipped. Building a filtered copy from scratch creates all-new nodes, so a comparison that is normally cheap becomes a comparison of every entry.
- Removing most keys from a persistent tree one at a time copies a path through the tree for every removal. That explains much of the allocator time in this profile.
- Tokio's default of one worker per CPU suits CPU-heavy servers. On a 120-vCPU machine running a mostly-waiting daemon, the extra workers mainly add wake-ups.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Which sessions are in scope depends on more than each session's own record. It also depends on two shared inputs: sessions with active operations, and the ancestors of the opened parents. The update keeps a copy of both. When either one changes, it rechecks just the sessions that changed in it, which is why it can skip all the other records.
- Native agent ids begin with an owner prefix (`native:{len}:{owner}`). When a session enters or leaves scope, a range lookup on that prefix finds its agents without scanning all 858.

**The finding was correct.** When history evicted an old snapshot, its cached scoped view stayed in memory. That view could never be served again, and it kept the snapshot's records and transcripts alive. Up to 32 such views could build up after large updates.

**The fix** (fd04b1bc5): every time a snapshot is added to history, the daemon also drops any scoped view whose snapshot has been evicted. A new test serves a view, forces eviction, and checks that the view is gone. That test fails when the fix is removed. The feed tests (11) and clippy pass.
